prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports the aisle geometry: shelving is in front of the wearer, with nearer shelf edges rendered brighter and the recessed aisle, wall, and gaps between units darker; the nearest shelving appears roughly 0.5–1.5 m away, while the back wall and farther fixtures are several metres away. Across the five frames, the viewpoint turns or moves rightward along the aisle, bringing the large shelf from the right side toward the centre and exposing different shelf faces; no clear person-shaped depth region is consistently visible, including where the RGB briefly shows a partly cropped person near the right edge of frame 1. It makes the shelves' layered depth, protruding edges, and partial occlusion of products easier to see than in RGB, but it does not reliably separate individual packages or provide metric distances. Several shelf surfaces are smeared together, and the black regions and abrupt discontinuities near frame borders, reflective surfaces, and thin shelf edges appear unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies only one small region labelled "book" on the left side of frame 1, roughly 1–2 m in front of the camera and below the camera's midline; it provides no masks for the shelves, packaged goods, wall, or the partly visible person in the RGB. If taken literally, the mask places the object left of the person and in front of the nearby shelving, but its shape and location overlap the shelf area and do not clearly correspond to a distinct book in RGB. Frames 2–5 are entirely unsegmented despite containing prominent shelves and many objects, so the map cannot support reliable distances, inter-object spacing, facing direction, reachability, occlusion tracking, or motion across the sequence. The isolated "book" label therefore appears unreliable, possibly a false detection or a shelf/product region assigned the wrong class.
descriptions.pose: The pose map shows a single yellow skeleton in frame 1, left of centre and roughly 1–2 m ahead, with an approximately horizontal torso-like chain and a vertical limb-like chain; no magenta hand skeletons appear. The RGB does contain a partly cropped person farther to the right in frame 1, but the plotted skeleton lies over the shelf area rather than matching that person's visible body, so its position, orientation, facing direction, and apparent reach are unreliable. No pose is detected in frames 2–5, and the map therefore shows no supported approach, retreat, turning, gaze toward the wearer, or changing occlusion. Although a valid pose map could expose joint arrangement and arm's-reach relationships that RGB obscures, this detection appears to be a false pose on shelf geometry and should not be used to infer a person's location.
